summary: Slovenia lies in southern Central Europe, where the Alps meet the Adriatic Sea; in 1991 it was the first to become independent from Yugoslavia, and it is known for Lake Bled and its cave landscapes.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Duchy of Carantania, founded in the 8th century by the ancestors of the Slovenes, was influenced by Bavaria and the Frankish kingdom, and missionaries from Salzburg and Aquileia led them to accept Catholicism. The area then belonged to the Habsburg dynasty for a long time (1278–1918); Protestantism appeared in the 16th century, but around 1600 it was re-Catholicized under the Counter-Reformation led by Bishop Tomaž Hren. Under Austrian rule the Catholic Church protected the Slovene language, and so it is closely bound up with national identity; it was suppressed in the Yugoslav communist period and regained its position after independence, but the share of believers keeps falling.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: From 1945 to 1991 the Yugoslav communist regime pursued secularization, weakening the church's role in education and society. Slovenia was the wealthiest and most urbanized republic of Yugoslavia, and after independence in 1991 it quickly integrated into Western Europe, so religious participation among the younger generation is very low. In practice many nominal Catholics no longer go to church either, so the number of non-believers may be higher than the statistics show.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Muslims are mainly laborers who came to Slovenia to work from other Yugoslav republics such as Bosnia and Kosovo in the 1960s–1980s, and their descendants. Because for a long time there was no formal mosque, believers could pray only in temporary premises, until the first mosque was completed in the capital, Ljubljana, in 2020, symbolizing the formal integration of this community.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Orthodox believers are mainly Serb laborers who moved in from Serbia and Bosnia during the Yugoslav period and their descendants; the Serbian Orthodox church in Ljubljana was built in the 1930s. In addition, in the 16th century, to defend against the Ottoman Empire, the Habsburg dynasty settled Orthodox refugees in the southern border region of Bela Krajina, leaving a small historical community.

religion.background: The Slovenes accepted Catholicism in the 8th century through missionaries from Salzburg and Aquileia. In the 16th century the Protestant reformer Primož Trubar published the first book in Slovene, but the Counter-Reformation soon made Catholicism the mainstream again. Under Habsburg rule the Catholic Church and the Slovene language together sustained the national culture. Secularization was pursued in communist Yugoslavia, and religious freedom was restored after independence in 1991, but society as a whole has already become highly secularized.

language.official: Slovene is the official language, and Italian and Hungarian are also recognized in certain areas.

ranking.name: Slovene
ranking.description: Slovene belongs to the South Slavic branch; the Freising Manuscripts, written around the year 1000, are among the earliest Slavic-language documents written in the Latin alphabet. In 1550 Trubar published the first book in Slovene, and in 1584 Dalmatin translated the complete Bible, laying the foundation of the written language; under Habsburg rule German long predominated, and in the 19th century poets such as Prešeren promoted the national revival. After independence in 1991 it became the national language, and although there are dozens of dialects within the country, almost all citizens have it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Serbo-Croatian
ranking.description: Its speakers are mostly immigrants who came to work in Slovenian factories from Yugoslav republics such as Croatia, Serbia and Bosnia in the 1960s–1980s, and their descendants. In the Yugoslav period Serbo-Croatian was the common language of the federation; after independence in 1991 the status of these languages fell, and some immigrants were even "erased" from the residents' register in 1992, causing years of controversy. Today most second-generation immigrants have switched to Slovene.

language.history: Slovene belongs to the South Slavic branch, and the Freising Manuscripts are among the oldest surviving documents. During the 16th-century Reformation, Trubar, Dalmatin and others published books and a Bible, laying the standard written language. Under Habsburg rule German was the language of the upper class and administration, Slovene was used mainly in the countryside and the church, and its status was raised only by the 19th-century national revival movement. In the Yugoslav period it was one of the official languages of the federation, and after independence in 1991 it became the national language; the Italian-speaking area on the coast and the Hungarian-speaking area in the northeast also enjoy local official status.

ranking.name: Potica
ranking.description: Fermented dough is rolled thin, spread with a filling such as walnut, honey or tarragon, rolled into a long roll and baked in a round mold, and when cut shows a beautiful spiral pattern.
ranking.history: Written records of potica go back to the 16th century; at first it was a luxury pastry that only nobles and monasteries could afford, and only later did it spread to the countryside. It is the star of the Slovenian Easter and Christmas tables, traditionally baked in a ceramic round mold, and each family has its own filling recipes, said to number in the dozens. Today it is regarded as Slovenia's most representative festival dessert and is also often given as a state gift to foreign guests.

ranking.name: Kranjska klobasa (Carniolan sausage)
ranking.description: A smoked sausage made of pork and a little bacon and seasoned with garlic and pepper, usually heated and eaten with sauerkraut, mustard and bread.
ranking.history: This sausage is named after Carniola, the historical region in central Slovenia that long belonged to the Habsburg dynasty. Folk legend says that Emperor Franz Joseph tasted it at an inn in Carniola and exclaimed in praise that it was a "Carniolan sausage," and its fame then spread through Vienna. In 2015 it obtained EU protected geographical indication, but neighboring Austria also has a sausage of the same name, so the two countries have had a dispute over the name.

ranking.name: Prekmurska gibanica
ranking.description: A cake baked from many layers of thin pastry alternating with four fillings, poppy seed, cottage cheese, walnut and apple, with distinct layers, sweet and moist.
ranking.history: This layer cake comes from the northeastern region of Prekmurje, which belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary until 1919 and whose cuisine is deeply influenced by the Pannonian Plain. All four fillings are products of local farms, and traditionally it was made only on important occasions such as weddings and festivals. It is one of the few Slovenian desserts to obtain the EU's "Traditional Speciality Guaranteed" certification and is regarded as the pride of the Prekmurje region.

ranking.name: Idrijski žlikrofi
ranking.description: Small hat-shaped dumplings filled with mashed potato, onion, bacon and herbs, often served with a lamb sauce called bakalca or as a side dish.
ranking.history: These dumplings come from Idrija in the western mountains, which became an important European source of mercury after mercury ore was discovered there in the late 15th century. In the mining town, cheap and filling potato dumplings became a common household staple. In 2010 Idrijski žlikrofi became the first Slovenian food to obtain the EU's "Traditional Speciality Guaranteed", and they must be made following fixed rules on shape and size.

ranking.name: Jota stew
ranking.description: A thick soup stewed for a long time with beans, sauerkraut or sour turnip, potato and smoked pork, sour, salty and rich, very suitable for cold weather.
ranking.history: Jota is popular on the Karst plateau, along the Adriatic coast and in neighboring Trieste and Friuli in Italy, places that once all belonged to the Habsburg dynasty and whose cuisine blends Slavic, Italian and Austrian elements. Beans and sauerkraut are both cheap ingredients that can be kept for a long time, making it a winter staple of farmers and port workers. Today it is still a local dish shared by western Slovenia and northeastern Italy.
